title: Claim and Recognition: Harriet Tubman’s Pension Case
setting: Washington, D.C., during the congressional handling of Harriet Tubman Davis’s pension claim, 1898-1899
description: A document-based historical adventure about how Congress judged Harriet Tubman’s Civil War service and why her pension was finally granted on a narrower basis.
learningObjectives: Describe the services Harriet Tubman performed for the Union during the Civil War.
Explain how Congress handled her pension claim and on what basis it was finally granted.
Evaluate whether Congress officially acknowledged her service.

player.name: Unnamed Clerk
player.brief: You sort claims, compare evidence, and prepare recommendations for lawmakers.

sharedContext.text: Harriet Tubman asked Congress to weigh her Civil War work as a nurse, cook, and spy. Yet the record says she finally secured a pension only as a widow of a Civil War veteran. As a House clerk, you must read the file, trace the claim, and decide what kind of recommendation to send forward.

spans.quote: Although her service as a nurse, cook, and spy for the federal government is less well known than her work on the Underground Railroad, it was on that basis that she requested a federal pension after the War.

Despite the endorsements of a number of highly ranked Civil War officials indicating the breadth of her service, Tubman ultimately secured a pension only as a widow of a Civil War veteran, not on the basis of her own service.

endings.title: A Narrow Victory
endings.summary: Your office accepts a pension increase on a narrower legal basis. Tubman receives help, but her own service is not fully acknowledged in the way you hoped.

historicalOutcome.text: This matches the record. Congress later passed an act for Harriet Tubman Davis, but the summary says she secured a pension only as a widow of a Civil War veteran, not on the basis of her own service.

spans.quote: An Act Granting and Increase in Pension to Harriet Tubman Davis, February 28, 1899;
Tubman ultimately secured a pension only as a widow of a Civil War veteran, not on the basis of her own service.

endings.divergence: This ending matches the record as summarized in the uploaded pages.
reflectionQuestions: Why might lawmakers have accepted a narrower legal basis instead of recognizing Tubman’s own service directly?
Does financial help count as full acknowledgment if the act avoids naming the service itself?
How did the House bill and the final outcome differ in what they seemed willing to recognize?

endings.title: Recognition Pushed Further
endings.summary: You push for open recognition of Tubman’s own Civil War service. Your recommendation goes beyond what the summary says Congress finally did.

historicalOutcome.text: The record points another way. The summary says Tubman secured a pension only as a widow of a Civil War veteran, not on the basis of her own service, even after endorsements and a bill naming service.

spans.quote: Despite the endorsements of a number of highly ranked Civil War officials indicating the breadth of her service, Tubman ultimately secured a pension only as a widow of a Civil War veteran, not on the basis of her own service.
H.R. 4982, a bill granting a pension to Harriet Tubman Davis, late a nurse in the U.S. Army, January 19, 1899;

endings.divergence: This ending differs from the record because it treats Tubman’s own service as the official basis for the pension.
reflectionQuestions: What evidence in the file supports stronger recognition of Tubman’s service?
Why might lawmakers still have refused to grant the pension on that basis?
How is moral recognition different from legal recognition?

endings.title: The File Stalls
endings.summary: You ask for more proof and delay a clear recommendation. The case remains unsettled in your version of events.

historicalOutcome.text: This differs from the record. The uploaded summary shows that Congress did move ahead to an act in 1899, even though Tubman’s own service was not the final basis named.

spans.quote: An Act Granting and Increase in Pension to Harriet Tubman Davis, February 28, 1899;
Tubman ultimately secured a pension only as a widow of a Civil War veteran, not on the basis of her own service.

endings.divergence: This ending differs from the record because the real case reached a final act instead of stopping at delay.
reflectionQuestions: What are the risks of delaying action when some evidence is already strong?
Would asking for more proof have protected fairness, or blocked recognition?
How do incomplete records shape what Congress is willing to say officially?
